The reviewer did not clear the last block. In hindsight it amounted to simulating a planned sharpening on stored per-sample attention, since a head's argmax pick is what infinite sharpening would produce. Predicting an edit's effect that way is not allowed. I'll set that question aside and measure the effect with a real pass instead, with the strength set by hand rather than derived from that analysis.

What I have legitimately is that L11h2 retrieves operands, and that operand misses come with diffuse retrieval (Spearman 0.56). The causal question is whether sharper retrieval attention in layer 11 improves operand choice in gold contexts.

In this architecture a per-head temperature cannot be changed through q_proj, because the per-head q_norm removes any uniform scaling. The cleanest lever is layer 11's k_norm, shared by its single key/value head: multiplying its effective gain (1+w) by α multiplies all four heads' attention logits by α. I'll start at α = 1.3, a moderate sharpening.

A gain in operand and result log-probability with little loss elsewhere would make retrieval focus a repairable bottleneck worth a generation test. A loss means the trained temperature is already right, and I'll close the line.

save_edit refused the k_norm change because it only rescales the norm's whole effective scale (1+w). Uniform attention-temperature changes count as out of scope, so the sharpening lever is closed by design. I won't work around it with a partial-dimension rescale, which would be an unjustified hack, and I'll correct the notes.

What remains legitimate on this mechanism is head-level scaling, which the rules list explicitly. Head 2's output enters layer 11's write alongside two mostly sink-attending heads (h0 and h1, which put 43-62% of their attention on BOS), and the post-attention norm divides that write by its RMS. So multiplying only head 2's o_proj columns by α raises the share of retrieved-number information in what layer 11 writes, without touching any other tensor. I'll screen α = 1.5 teacher-forced.

Better operand log-probabilities would support "retrieved operands are under-weighted" as a repairable failure. No change or a loss closes the retrieval line.

The last run confirmed that E4 is saved: the only edited tensor is layer 11's o_proj (640×1024), with head 2's columns 512:768 multiplied by 1.5. Before spending pass 8 on the teacher-forced screen, I need to recover two things after the restart. First, the exact request used for the earlier screens (passes 6 and 7, recorded in fwd_6/meta.json), so the edited pass lines up token for token with the original baselines. Second, the name of the screening function I wrote in reply 73. I'll also re-ground on the pass-1 baseline: accuracy by ending format, and how often a wrong answer contains the gold number somewhere, as the answer itself or inside a \boxed{} that the grader did not pick. A large "had it but lost it" share would point to a final-answer or format mechanism as a target. A small one means the misses are genuine reasoning errors.

Pass 1 baseline: the original model gets 12.5% of 512 DEV problems right. 29.5% of answers end with a usable "####" and 11.9% are cut at the token limit. Only 48 of the 389 wrong, finished answers contain the gold number anywhere, so most misses never compute the right value. That looks like genuine reasoning failure, not a corrupted final line. The earlier screens used token_logprobs with topk 1 on tf_screen.json, and my comparison function is `screen`, so pass 8 can reuse both.

One oddity is worth a cheap check before spending passes. Answers that contain "####" are less accurate (10.4%) than \boxed{} answers (17.3%). Two explanations are possible. "####" may be used as markdown headers ("#### Step 3: ...") that the grader mistakes for the final answer. Or the number written after "####" may contradict the model's own last computed result. If, in "####" answers, the number before the marker is often gold while the number after it is not, a final-answer mechanism becomes a concrete target. If the two agree, the gap reflects problem difficulty or style and I'll move on.
